title: Love close

segments.voice: Yesterday, different loves: agape, bhakti, metta, ishq, ren. Your line was many loves. Which one stayed with you? Today closes sixty days on love. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

A philosopher's ladder. A myth about humans split in two. A widow on a dusty road, refusing to turn back. A basin of water and a towel. A mother guarding her only child. A coat by the door that nobody can bring themselves to move. This block of sixty days opened with a handful of words for love and a question: one thing, or many? Before the hills turn to something new, look back once. Today: Diotima.
screen: `A LADDER. A ROAD. A TOWEL.` → `SIXTY DAYS ON LOVE.` → `LOOK BACK ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, the philosophers. In Plato's Symposium, Diotima teaches that love climbs, from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Aristotle calls a friend another self. Montaigne, asked why he loved his friend, could only say: because it was he, because it was I. Second, the scriptures. Ruth, to her mother-in-law Naomi: “whither thou goest, I will go.” Jesus kneels and washes his friends' feet. A letter of John puts it in three words: “God is love.” In the Qur'an, one of God's names is the Loving. Third, the small. Thérèse of Lisieux and her little way: the smallest actions, done for love. The Dhammapada's water-pot, filled drop by drop. The letter of James: “swift to hear, slow to speak.” Simone Weil, holding that attention is a rare and pure kind of generosity. Fourth, the turn these sixty days kept making. Again and again, the texts treated love less as a feeling that happens to you and more as something done. Keeping a friendship from fading. Listening without fixing. Letting a grown child go. Sitting with grief. Writing the note. The traditions disagree about a great deal, and their loves stay different, as yesterday showed. But the texts we read kept coming back to hands and feet: a towel, a road, a cup of water, a word said out loud. Love, in these sixty days, has mostly been a verb.
screen: `THE PHILOSOPHERS: IT CLIMBS.` · `THE SCRIPTURES: IT KNEELS.` · `THE SMALL: IT STARTS CLOSE.` · `IT IS SOMETHING DONE.` · then, large: `LOVE IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one person who hasn't heard it from you lately. Maybe it's obvious; maybe it's someone you'd never think to tell. Let their face come clear. Now let the words form, as plainly as you'd say them: I love you. Or, if that isn't how your family talks, the version that is. Thanks for being you. I'm glad you're my brother. I think about you. Hold the words, and picture saying them. After the bell, you can tell them: out loud, in a message, or with a hand on the shoulder. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.

Diotima, the philosopher in Plato's Symposium who teaches that love climbs from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Sixty days on love, from her philosopher's ladder to a note on paper, ending where it kept landing: in what we do. Today's word.
Your line: love is the practice. Today, tell one person you love them, plainly, in whatever way your people say it. Tomorrow, the hills turn to work. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Traditions keep love through practice: Christians through service and prayer, Buddhists through loving-kindness meditation and small daily good deeds, and friends and families by saying it out loud.
